strengths: Identifies a concrete, counterintuitive failure mode (non-monotonic budget scaling) with a clear mechanistic explanation via trajectory drift
Proposes a simple and well-motivated fix (chunked allocation with M=1) that directly addresses the diagnosed root cause
Quantitative claims are specific and falsifiable (60.5% failure attribution, 25× success rate improvement, 98.4% degenerate calibration rate)
Connects the failure mode to a broader structural principle (sequential vs. parallel budget use) that could generalize beyond web agents
weaknesses: The proposed solution—spend all budget in one round (M=1)—is trivially derived from the diagnosis; the intellectual contribution is thin once trajectory drift is named
The extremely low baseline success rate (0.86%) raises concerns about the experimental setup; the 25× headline figure may be misleading if the baseline is pathological rather than representative

The third contribution bullet reveals that world-model calibration is so poor (p̂=0 for 98.4% of cycles) that it calls into question whether the underlying approach is viable at all, yet this concern is not addressed
Scope is narrow (web checkout in one benchmark); generalizability claims are implicit rather than empirically supported
No discussion of why parallel rollouts are feasible at the same budget cost as sequential ones, or of latency/compute tradeoffs

ai_detection.reasoning: The introduction follows a highly formulaic structure: one-paragraph background, one-paragraph problem statement with a named phenomenon, a 'key insight' pivot paragraph, and a clean four-bullet contributions list with precise statistics. The prose is uniformly terse and declarative with no rhetorical variation, hedging, or discursive digressions typical of human academic writing. The single-anchor prior work pattern (Li et al., 2025 doing most framing work) and the clinical 'Our contributions are:' enumeration are strong AI-generation signals.
